intro: Tilburg is probably named after a lime tree, and the lime is not there any more. One stood on the Heuvel from about 1598, so wide that a visitor in 1667 counted 62 paces around the crown and 28 pillars holding it up. It was felled in 1994 against loud protest, and three of its descendants were planted on the square in 2009. So this page is the trees that survived instead: the oldest elm in the city, two in a park dug by unemployed men in the 1930s, and a lime that outlived the famous one by thirty years.
meta_description: Twenty remarkable trees in Tilburg: the city's oldest elm, two in Leonard Springer's last park, and the story of the lime the city may be named after.
question_meta: Tilburg's oldest surviving tree is a silver lime at the Frater Paullussehof, banded 1830 to 1840. The famous Heuvel lime was felled in 1994.
question_answer: The oldest tree still standing in Tilburg is a silver lime at the Frater Paullussehof, which the national register places in a planting band of 1830 to 1840, so somewhere approaching two centuries. The question is complicated by the tree most people mean when they ask it. A lime stood on the Heuvel, the city's central square, from about 1598, and it was cut down in 1994 at roughly five hundred years old. When the stump was lifted it turned out to be hollow, with a young shoot growing inside it from its own root. Three descendants of that tree were planted on the rearranged Heuvel on 26 March 2009, so there is a lime on the square again, but it is seventeen years old rather than five hundred.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every age on this page is a band and none has been narrowed to look precise. The register is the 2024 edition and is the single source for most of these trees, which is why they are flagged. It is also why the Heuvel lime is not on this page: the register still carries an entry for a lime on the Heuvel with a planting band of 1600 to 1700, and that tree has been gone since 1994. We checked it rather than publishing it, and that check is the reason to treat every old register entry as a claim rather than a fact. If you go to one of these and find it has gone the same way, tell us and it comes off the same day. Pins marked approximate mean we know the park and not the trunk.

faq.q: What happened to the famous lime tree on the Heuvel?
faq.a: It was felled in 1994, after standing since about 1598, despite heavy protest. The crane lifted a hollow stump with a young shoot growing inside it from the tree's own root. On 26 March 2009 three descendants were planted on the rebuilt square, so there is a lime on the Heuvel again, just not that one.

faq.q: Is Tilburg really named after a lime tree?
faq.a: It is a plausible reading rather than a settled one. Tilia is the Latin for lime, and the tree on the Heuvel was the town's unofficial symbol for centuries, with justice pronounced under it. The etymology is argued about; the association is not.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Tilburg now?
faq.a: A silver lime at the Frater Paullussehof, banded 1830 to 1840 by the national register. The elm in the Wilhelminapark is the oldest elm in the city and, according to the register, was already standing before the park was laid out around it.

All twenty. The Wilhelminapark and the Leijpark are open public parks, the Korvelplein is a square, the two limes stand in public planting, the Zuiderpark trees line an ordinary residential street, and the twin planes stand on the open Stadhuisplein behind the town hall. Nothing here has a gate or a charge.

trees.name: The Oldest Elm of Tilburg
trees.age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880

location.address: Wilhelminapark, in the south corner of the park

trees.story:
The register says two things about this tree and both are worth having. It is the oldest elm in Tilburg, and it was already standing before the park was laid out around it.

That second fact is the interesting one. A park built around an existing tree is a different object from a park planted from nothing: somebody stood on this ground, looked at what was here, and drew the paths to keep it. The elm was the reason for a decision rather than the result of one.

Being the oldest elm anywhere in the Netherlands is a harder thing than it sounds. Dutch elm disease arrived here in the 1920s and the second, far more aggressive strain in the 1970s, and between them they killed most of the mature elms in the country. Whole avenues went. An elm that reached a century and a half through both waves did so partly by luck of position, standing alone in a park corner rather than in a line where the beetles could work along it.

It is in the south corner. Elms leaf late and hold on late, so in November it is often still green when the rest of the park has turned.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the south corner, with the asymmetric leaf base elms have, one side of the leaf starting lower on the stalk than the other.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Frater Paullussehof
trees.age_estimate: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840

location.address: Frater Paullussehof 141

trees.story:
The oldest tree standing in Tilburg is a lime, which in a town that may be named after a lime is a decent piece of luck, and it is not on the square where anyone would look for it.

Silver lime is worth learning to recognise, because the trick is easy and it works from thirty metres. The underside of every leaf is coated in fine white felt, so on a windy day the whole crown flickers between deep green and pale silver as the leaves turn over. No other large lime does this.

It has a second habit that is less charming. Silver lime flowers late, in July, and its nectar is famously hard on bumblebees; you sometimes find them stunned or dead under a big one in high summer. The mechanism has been argued over for decades and the current reading is that it is less about toxicity than about a starving late-season insect finding a huge, tempting, low-yield food source at the wrong moment.

So: go in July for the scent, which is heavy and carries a long way down a street, and look at the ground while you are there.
trees.access: Free. Public planting in a residential courtyard, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km northwest of Tilburg station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: A big lime whose leaves flash white underneath in any breeze.

best_time.label: July, when the whole tree smells of honey from a street away

trees.name: The Canadian Poplar of the Wilhelminapark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: Wilhelminapark, in the northeast corner of the park

trees.story:
Poplars are not supposed to get this old, which is the entire reason to go and look at this one.

Canadian poplar is a hybrid of the European black poplar and the American eastern cottonwood, first raised in France in the eighteenth century and then planted across Europe by the million for the same reason people plant it now: it grows faster than almost anything else, throwing up several feet a year on wet ground. The trade-off is that it is soft-timbered, brittle in storms and generally treated as a crop rather than a monument. A hundred years is a good run. Most are taken out well before that because a limb has come down.

This one is somewhere past a century and a half and still standing in the northeast corner of the park, which means it has been through every serious storm since the 1860s without losing enough to condemn it.

The sound is the other thing. Poplar leaves are held on flattened stalks that let the blade pivot, so the whole crown rattles in wind that barely moves the trees beside it. On a breezy day you hear this one before you see it.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The tallest tree in the northeast corner, with a crown that rattles audibly in light wind.

trees.name: The Sessile Oak of the Korvelplein
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910

location.address: Korvelplein 200

trees.story:
In 1923 they took the church off this square.

The old Korvel church stood in the middle of the Korvelplein. It was removed and replaced by a new one built at the edge, which left a large empty space in a busy district, and the response was to plant it properly with trees. This oak is one of those, and the register bands it slightly earlier, 1900 to 1910, so it may have been standing before the clearance and been kept.

It is a sessile oak rather than the pedunculate oak that turns up everywhere else in the Netherlands, and the difference is easy once you know it. Pedunculate oak hangs its acorns on long stalks and has almost no stalk on the leaf. Sessile oak does the reverse: acorns sitting tight against the twig, leaves on a clear stalk of a centimetre or more. Sessile is the upland species, the one that prefers drier and poorer ground.

A square is a hard place to be a tree. Paving over the roots, salt in winter, cars, and a hundred and twenty years of it. This one has managed, and the Korvelplein is one of the more pleasant squares in the city because of trees like it.
trees.access: Free. Public square, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Tilburg station, on foot or a short bus ride to Korvel.
trees.how_to_recognise: An old oak on the square with acorns sitting tight to the twig and leaves on a clear stalk.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Leijpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 85 to 95 years, from the register's planting band of 1930 to 1940

location.address: Leijpark, centrally in the park, Professor van Bruchemlaan 2

trees.story:
This park was dug by unemployed men.

Leonard Springer, the most sought-after garden architect in the Netherlands, drew the Leijpark in 1919 as his last large design. Then nothing happened for fifteen years: the land could not be bought and there was a farm sitting in the middle of it. It was finally laid out between 1934 and 1939 as a work relief project, in the depths of the depression, thirty hectares in the English landscape manner along the little river Leij that gives it its name.

So this silver maple was planted by men who were there because there was no other work. Springer designed the picture and never saw it finished.

Silver maple is another American import chosen for speed, and it has the finest-cut leaf of any maple you will meet here, deeply divided into five narrow lobes with silvery-white undersides. It flowers absurdly early, in March, before any leaf, small red and yellow tufts straight on the bare twigs. It is one of the first trees in the park to do anything at all after winter.

Stand in the middle of the park and it is the one with the pale flickering crown.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.
trees.how_to_recognise: Deeply cut five-lobed leaves that show silver-white underneath, centrally in the park.

best_time.label: March, when it flowers on bare twigs before anything else moves

trees.name: The Oak of the Leijpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 85 to 95 years, from the register's planting band of 1930 to 1940

location.address: Leijpark, on the northwest side, Professor van Bruchemlaan 2

trees.story:
The youngest tree on this page and the one that will outlast every other by centuries.

It went in with the rest of the Leijpark planting between 1934 and 1939, part of the work relief scheme that finally built Springer's 1919 design. At under a century it is barely started. Pedunculate oak routinely reaches four hundred years in the Netherlands and the veterans on sandy ground in Brabant go beyond that, which means the silver maple beside it, the poplar in the Wilhelminapark and the elm in the south corner will all be gone while this one is still filling out.

That is a genuinely strange thing to stand in front of. A park laid out in a depression by men who needed the wages, planted with trees on wildly different clocks, and the plainest one in it is the one making the long bet.

It is on the northwest side, in Springer's English landscape arrangement of grass opening into stands of trees. Come in October: an oak this age is producing serious quantities of acorns, and the ground under it is worth looking at.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad oak on the northwest side of the park, with acorns on long stalks.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns are down

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Villa Garden
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Park on the Fokkerpad, opposite number 11

trees.story:
This small park was somebody's garden, designed by Leonard Springer.

That is all the register says about it, and it is enough to change how the place reads. Springer laid out estates, cemeteries, arboreta and the Leijpark on the other side of town, and he also took private commissions from people building villas. A garden of that kind was made to be walked in by one family. This one ended up as public ground, which is the usual fate of a nineteenth century villa garden in a city that grew past it.

The lime is from that planting, banded 1880 to 1890. Silver lime was a favourite of designers in exactly this period, because it does something no other large tree does: the white-felted undersides of the leaves make the whole crown pale and unsettled whenever there is wind, so a single one placed against darker trees lifts a composition without any need for flowers.

So look at it as a piece of design rather than as a specimen. It is standing where a professional put it, for a reason he could have explained, in a garden whose owner is long gone and whose gate is now open to everyone.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Tilburg station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The lime with white-backed leaves, standing against the darker planting of the old villa garden.

best_time.label: July, when the scent fills the whole garden

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of the Zuiderpark Collection
trees.age_estimate: roughly 70 years

location.address: Morvanstraat 14, plantsoen

trees.story:
For seventeen years, up to a thousand students a season walked this path and had to name what they saw. Between 1953 and 1967, adult evening students training as horticulturists and florists were examined here, quizzed on the Latin and Dutch names of trees along a route locals nicknamed the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane, for how it felt to be tested on your feet in front of an instructor. This Caucasian wingnut, one of the trees they were made to know, still rings the site of the municipal nursery that trained them.

The register misnames it in its own Dutch, calling it a 'Japanese wingnut' though the species it maps is Pterocarya fraxinifolia, the Caucasian kind. That is a small irony for a tree planted to teach people exactly this. Planted in the 1950s, it is young by this project's ordinary standard, in its seventies rather than its centuries, and its case for a page rests on its history rather than its age: a rare-species teaching collection is not something Tilburg has anywhere else.

In 1967 the school moved elsewhere and the sweat lane went quiet. The trees it left behind, planted street trees in an ordinary residential corner of Zuiderpark, are free to see any time, no lane, no exam, no waiting for your turn.
trees.access: Free. Public street planting (plantsoen), open at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km south of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1697210) is the only source naming this specific tree; existence/species/age are single-sourced, hence flagged. Register's own name is 'Japanse vleugelnoot' but the mapped species field is Caucasian Wingnut, Pterocarya fraxinifolia. Planted band 1950-1960. Part of a documented rare-tree teaching collection (former gemeentekwekerij on the Tatraweg); wikimiddenbrabant.nl independently corroborates the shared school history (1967 relocation, 1974 merger) though not this individual tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the Caucasian wingnut once used to test trainee horticulturists along the old 'sweat lane' route. It stands at Morvanstraat 14, in the street planting strip.

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.name: The American Yellowwood of the Zuiderpark Collection
trees.age_estimate: roughly 70 years

location.address: Harzstraat 2, plantsoen

trees.story:
Its Dutch name gives away the trick before you have seen it: geelhout, yellow wood, because the wood beneath the bark of a cut branch runs bright yellow. This American yellowwood is another of the specimens planted around Tilburg's old municipal nursery in the 1950s, where evening students of horticulture and floristry were drilled on tree names along what they called the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane.

Cladrastis kentukea is native to the American south and rare in Dutch planting, which is presumably the whole reason the nursery grew it: something a florist would otherwise never meet. Multi-stemmed and now in its seventies, it flowers in May and June with hanging white clusters, then turns gold in autumn, living up to the name a second time.

Like the rest of the Zuiderpark collection, its record is thin: a single register entry with no independent account of the tree itself, only of the school that once stood around it. The teaching moved elsewhere in 1967 and the students stopped coming, but a scatter of trees they were quizzed on is still rooted in this ordinary residential corner, free to walk past on an afternoon nobody has to pass an exam for.
trees.access: Free. Public street planting (plantsoen), open at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km south of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1697211, register_name 'Geelhout Zuiderpark') is the only source naming this tree, hence flagged. 'Geelhout' is the standard Dutch common name for Cladrastis kentukea, cross-checked against Dutch nursery/dendrology references for the species mapping only. Planted band 1950-1960, multi-stemmed. Same rare-tree teaching-collection history as til_008.

best_time.label: May and June, when hanging white flower clusters drape the crown

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the multi-stemmed trunk and, in May and June, hanging white flower clusters that turn gold in autumn. It stands in the plantsoen at Harzstraat 2.

trees.name: The Pecan of the Zuiderpark Collection
trees.age_estimate: roughly 70 years

location.address: Morvanstraat 14, plantsoen

trees.story:
A pecan tree in Tilburg is already the story. Carya illinoinensis belongs to the warm river valleys of the American south and Mexico, and one has been growing on this ordinary Zuiderpark street corner since the 1950s, part of the same rare-tree collection planted around the city's old municipal nursery to give trainee horticulturists something unfamiliar to learn.

Whether it has ever produced a usable nut this far from home is not recorded, and the register that is the only source for this tree says nothing about it beyond species, age band and location. What the register does confirm is that the nursery deliberately sought out trees like this: species nobody training as a Dutch florist or gardener would otherwise encounter, planted along a path its evening students nicknamed the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane, for the oral exams held on it between 1953 and 1967.

The teaching stopped when the school moved to a different site in 1967, and the trees it left scattered through this corner of the neighbourhood are the only evidence it ever existed. This one shares its street corner with a Caucasian wingnut a few paces away, part of the same quiet collection, free to see, no ticket, no exam.
trees.access: Free. Public street planting (plantsoen), open at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km south of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1697207, register_name 'Pecannoot Zuiderpark') is the only source naming this tree, hence flagged. Planted band 1950-1960. Same rare-tree teaching-collection history as til_008; same address as til_008, a few metres apart.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the pecan in the same rare-tree collection as the Caucasian wingnut nearby. It stands at Morvanstraat 14, in the street planting strip.

trees.name: The Transcaucasian Birch of the Zuiderpark Collection
trees.age_estimate: roughly 70 years

location.address: Harzstraat 26, plantsoen

trees.story:
Most Transcaucasian birches grown in cultivation are shrubs, wide and many-stemmed rather than trees with a single climbing trunk. This one, planted in the 1950s on an ordinary Zuiderpark street corner, is recorded by the national tree register in its natural form, which if the record is accurate makes it a rarity twice over: an uncommon species grown in an uncommon shape.

Betula medwediewii comes from the mountain forests of the Caucasus, and like its neighbours on this street it was planted to be studied rather than admired: part of a rare-species collection that once ringed Tilburg's municipal plant nursery, where evening students training as horticulturists and florists were examined on tree names along a route they called the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane, between 1953 and 1967.

The register is this tree's only source, so its shape and exact age carry the honest caveat of a single account. What is certain is that it is roughly seventy years old, standing where a school once trained hundreds of students a year in exactly the skill of telling one tree from another, a skill now free for anyone to skip: just walk past and look.
trees.access: Free. Public street planting (plantsoen), open at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km south of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1697206, register_name 'Transkaukasische berk Zuiderpark') is the only source naming this tree, hence flagged. Dutch nursery sources independently confirm 'Transkaukasische berk' maps to Betula medwediewii, usually a multi-stemmed shrub in cultivation; register's own 'form' field says natural form here. Planted band 1950-1960. Same rare-tree teaching-collection history as til_008.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its single climbing trunk, unusual for a species normally grown as a wide, many-stemmed shrub. It stands in the plantsoen at Harzstraat 26.

trees.name: The Golden Beech of the Zuiderpark Collection
trees.age_estimate: roughly 70 years

location.address: Morvanstraat 22, plantsoen

trees.story:
This beech spends its whole year doing what most trees save for October. Fagus sylvatica 'Zlatia' is a golden-leaved cultivar bred to hold colour rather than wait for autumn to produce it: its leaves emerge bright yellow in spring, settle to a softer yellow-green through summer, then brighten to yellow again as the season turns, so the crown never really goes green at all.

It stands on a Zuiderpark street corner, planted in the 1950s as part of a rare-tree teaching collection that once surrounded Tilburg's municipal plant nursery, where evening students of horticulture and floristry were quizzed on tree names along a path nicknamed the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane, until the school relocated in 1967.

Roughly seventy years old now, its only record is the national tree register, so treat the details as flagged rather than double checked. What a visitor gets regardless is the rarest thing this small collection has to offer: a tree that looks like it is always about to turn, in a residential corner of the city built to teach exactly that kind of looking.
trees.access: Free. Public street planting (plantsoen), open at any time.
trees.transport: About 2 km south of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1697209, register_name 'Goudbeuk Zuiderpark') is the only source naming this tree, hence flagged. 'Goudbeuk' confirmed by Dutch nursery references as the standard name for Fagus sylvatica 'Zlatia'. Planted band 1950-1960. Same rare-tree teaching-collection history as til_008.

best_time.label: April and May, when the new leaves come in bright gold

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by leaves that stay yellow all season instead of turning green, brightest in spring and again in autumn. It stands in the plantsoen at Morvanstraat 22.

trees.name: The Kloosterpark Oak
trees.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own register name (kloosterparkeik); ask the reader which oak
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years

location.address: Leijpark, Kloosterpark corner, far northeast of the park off Ringbaan-Zuid

trees.story:
The name gives away a building that is no longer there. This oak's register entry calls it the kloosterparkeik, the cloister-park oak, for a convent that stood on this ground until its garden was redeveloped and folded into the wider Leijpark. The convent, home to the Congregatie van Onze Lieve Vrouw der Afzondering in het Cenakel, was founded here in 1908, close to when this tree is thought to have gone in.

Two tall black residential towers now stand where the convent's own garden once did, built after the land was sold on. The oak survived that whole transition, tucked into the far northeast corner of the Leijpark in what is still locally called the Kloosterparkbos, a patch of wood the wider park's paths were simply extended to include rather than replace.

The Leijpark itself, 30 hectares designed by Leonard Springer in 1919 and built between 1934 and 1939 as unemployment relief work once land negotiations finally cleared, is well documented; this corner and its convent past rest on the tree register alone, so treat that part as a good story rather than a settled fact. The register cannot say which oak it is, so that stays an open question for whoever visits next. Free, open daily, an easy add to the existing Leijpark walk.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1695664, register_name 'kloosterparkeik') is the only source naming this tree; no species beyond 'oak' given. Planted band 1900-1910. Convent history (Congregatie van Onze Lieve Vrouw der Afzondering in het Cenakel, founded 1908) is register-only; the wider Leijpark's designer, size and 1934-1939 work-relief construction are independently corroborated by nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leijpark. Sits within about 30m of til_014 and til_015.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: tucked into the wooded Kloosterparkbos, the far northeast corner of the Leijpark, near two tall black residential towers.

trees.name: The Kloosterpark Lime
trees.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own register name (kloosterparklinde); ask the reader which lime
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years

location.address: Leijpark, Kloosterpark corner, far northeast of the park off Ringbaan-Zuid

trees.story:
Thirty metres from the cloister-park oak stands its neighbour with the matching name: the kloosterparklinde, the cloister-park lime, both named for a convent whose garden this ground used to be before it was absorbed into the Leijpark. The Congregatie van Onze Lieve Vrouw der Afzondering in het Cenakel founded its convent here in 1908, and this lime is thought to have been planted within a decade or so of that, making it roughly 120 years old today.

The wider park around it is well recorded: Leonard Springer designed the 30-hectare Leijpark in 1919, though it took until 1934 to 1939 to actually build it, as unemployment relief work once the land itself had finally been assembled. This tree's own corner, tucked in the park's far northeast reach and still known locally as the Kloosterparkbos, is documented only in the national tree register, which does not say which kind of lime it is, so that stays a question for a visitor with sharper eyes than a register entry.

Standing beside an oak and a large-leaved holly of the same age and the same forgotten convent, it makes a short, easy extension to the Leijpark walk already published on this page. Free, open daily, no ticket.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1695665, register_name 'kloosterparklinde') is the only source naming this tree; no species beyond 'lime' given. Planted band 1900-1910. Same Kloosterpark/convent history as til_013; the wider Leijpark's designer, size and 1934-1939 construction are independently corroborated by nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leijpark. About 30m from til_013 and til_015.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the cloister-park lime, standing 30 metres from its oak neighbour of the same name. It stands at the Kloosterpark corner of Leijpark.

trees.name: The Kloosterpark Holly
trees.species_basis: register gives only the Dutch descriptive name (grootbladige kloosterparkhulst); Ilex x altaclerensis and Ilex latifolia are both large-leaved candidates, ask the reader which
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years

location.address: Leijpark, Kloosterpark corner, far northeast of the park off Ringbaan-Zuid

trees.story:
Holly rarely gets old enough to earn a place on a page like this one, which is what makes this specimen worth the detour. Tucked in the same forgotten corner of the Leijpark as its oak and lime neighbours, all three named for a convent that stood here until the early twentieth century, this large-leaved holly is thought to be around 120 years old, an unusual age and size for a species usually seen as garden hedging rather than a tree in its own right.

The national register that is its only record calls it simply grootbladige kloosterparkhulst, the large-leaved cloister-park holly, without settling which large-leaved species it actually is: Ilex x altaclerensis and Ilex latifolia are both candidates, and a visitor who can tell the two apart would be doing this page a favour.

The convent itself, home to the Congregatie van Onze Lieve Vrouw der Afzondering in het Cenakel from 1908, is long gone, its garden folded into the wider Leijpark when the land was redeveloped. What is left is this quiet triangle of three old trees at the park's far northeast edge, a five minute add to the existing walk, free and open daily, no ticket, no convent left to visit but the ground it once stood on.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km southeast of Tilburg station.
trees.verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1695666, register_name 'Grootbladige kloosterparkhulst') is the only source naming this tree; no settled species. Planted band 1900-1910, unusually old for a holly. Same Kloosterpark/convent history as til_013 and til_014. About 30m from both.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a holly grown into a full tree rather than clipped hedging, unusual at this size. It stands in the same forgotten corner of Leijpark as its oak and lime neighbours.

trees.name: The Marialinde of Oisterwijk
trees.age_estimate: over 650 years, and locally said to approach a thousand

location.address: De Lind, behind the Oude Raadhuis (Old Town Hall), Oisterwijk

trees.story:
The trunk you can put a hand on is younger than the tree. By the 19th century the Marialinde's original stem had rotted hollow, and the remedy of the period was to plant a spruce down inside the cavity, which is what was done here. The lime solved it differently. A root running down through its own hollow thickened, took over the job and became the trunk standing on De Lind today: the same individual tree, on its second stem, never replanted.

Its age depends on which evidence you believe. The paper trail reaches 1388, when damage to the tree by fire was written down. Dendrologists reading the wood favour a planting somewhere between 1600 and 1700. Oisterwijk itself will tell you the lime is about a thousand years old, in the tone of a town that has been saying so for generations. Nobody has reconciled the three.

What happened underneath it is better documented. A chapel holding a statue of Mary was set at the tree in the late 15th century and gave it the name it still carries. Justice was administered here. Cheese and eggs were sold in its shade on market days. In 2023 the country voted it Dutch Tree of the Year.

It stands behind the old town hall on the central square, trunk fenced, a bench around it, free to walk up to, ten minutes from Oisterwijk station.
trees.access: Free, standing on De Lind, Oisterwijk's central square, fenced at the trunk with a surrounding bench
trees.transport: Oisterwijk NS railway station, roughly 10-15 minutes' walk to the town centre

best_time.label: June into July, when the lime flowers and the square smells of it

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bench encircling its trunk, itself a root that grew down through the original hollow stem to become a second trunk. It stands on De Lind, behind the Oude Raadhuis in Oisterwijk.

trees.name: The Weeping Silver Lime of the Wilhelminapark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 128 years, planted in 1898 during Leonard Springer's original layout of the park

location.address: Wilhelminapark, in the northwest corner of the park

trees.story:
Most old park trees are dated by guesswork. This one has a date. The Dutch national monument register says it was planted in 1898 by Leonard Springer during his original layout of the Wilhelminapark, and the register's note names this tree rather than the scheme around it. The park opened to the public that same May.

Springer was designing the whole park from scratch, and a weeping silver lime is a deliberate choice rather than a tree you put in to fill a gap. Tilia tomentosa 'Petiolaris' lets its branches hang, and every leaf carries a coat of white felt on the underside, so a breeze turns the whole crown from green to silver and back in a second. The register records the form as kandelaber, candelabra: the crown was trained up on a frame of raised limbs rather than left to run. Roughly 128 years on, that decision is still the shape of the tree.

What nobody has written down is how big it has become. No girth or height figure exists for it in the register or in any other source we could find, which for a lime of this age is a gap a tape measure would close in a minute. If you take one, tell us.

It stands in the northwest corner. The elm in the south corner and the Canadian poplar in the northeast make the rest of a short loop, and the park holds twenty-two monumental trees in all.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hanging branches and the leaves that flash white underneath when the wind turns them. It stands in the northwest corner of the park, its crown trained up into a candelabra rather than left to run.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers late and the scent hangs in the corner of the park

verified_sources: netherlands-lrmb register (nr 1689276): planted_band 1890-1900, history note 'Geplant in 1898 door Leonard Springer bij aanleg park', form 'Kandelaber' (candelabra), owner gemeente, visitable ja, visible ja
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot (the same walk as the park's other monumental trees, til_001 and til_003).

trees.name: The Flowering Ash of the Wilhelminapark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 130 years, from the register's 1890-1900 planting band, planted during the park's original construction

location.address: Wilhelminapark, in the northwest corner of the park

trees.story:
The national register lists this tree and then admits you probably cannot see it. Its visibility field reads nee, no, which is an odd thing for a monument list to concede about a monument. The tree is there, in the northwest corner of the Wilhelminapark, planted with the rest of the park when Leonard Springer laid it out in the 1890s. Which trunk it is, among several similar trees standing close together in that corner, the register does not settle and neither can we. The pin here is honest about that: it puts you in the right corner and leaves you to look.

There is one stretch of the year when looking gets easy. Fraxinus ornus is not the common ash of Dutch roadsides. It is a smaller southern European relative that flowers, properly flowers, in May and June, throwing dense upright plumes of creamy white over the whole crown at once. The Dutch call it pluimes, plume ash; in English it also goes by manna ash. Nothing else in that corner of the park does anything close to it.

Its age comes from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900, which puts it near 130 years, the same generation as the park itself. Nobody has recorded its girth. If you find it, either a tape measure or a plain note saying which trunk it was would close a gap we cannot close from here.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in May and June by the upright plumes of creamy white flower, which nothing else in this corner carries. It stands in the northwest corner of the park; the register does not settle which of the trunks there it is.

best_time.label: May and June, when the whole crown goes over to upright plumes of creamy white

verified_sources: netherlands-lrmb register (nr 1695646): planted_band 1890-1900, register name 'Pluimes', history note 'Aangeplant bij de aanleg van het park door Leonard Springer', owner gemeente, visitable ja, visible nee
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot.

trees.name: The Pontic Oak of the Wilhelminapark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 50 years, from the register's 1970-1980 planting band

location.address: Wilhelminapark, southwest side of the park

trees.story:
The Dutch national register protects this one for a single stated reason, and the reason is not its age. The field reads dendrologisch. It is on the list for what it is, not for how long it has stood there.

Quercus pontica grows wild in one small pocket of northeast Turkey and the western Caucasus, and nowhere else. In Europe it turns up in botanic gardens and specialist collections; a municipal park where anyone can walk up to one on a Tuesday afternoon is an unusual address for it. It also refuses to behave like an oak. It stays low, a big shrub or a small tree rather than a spreading giant, and it comes up on several stems instead of a single trunk, which the register notes in its own form field as meerstammig. The leaves are the giveaway. They are far larger than any native Dutch oak's, stiff, deeply ribbed along parallel veins and saw-toothed round the edge, and held next to a pedunculate oak leaf they look like they belong to different genera.

The register's planting band is 1970 to 1980, so the tree is somewhere around fifty, an infant beside the 1898 plantings it shares the park with. No girth figure exists for it in any source we could reach directly. Go for the leaves and for the oddity of finding this species growing in a Dutch park at all, not for the years.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, far larger and more deeply ribbed than any native oak's, and by the several stems that come up together instead of one trunk. It stands low, on the southwest side of the park.
verified_sources: netherlands-lrmb register (nr 1689279): planted_band 1970-1980, reason 'dendrologisch', form 'Meerstammig' (multi-stemmed), owner gemeente, visitable ja, visible ja

monumentaltrees.com lists a dedicated page titled 'Pontische eik in het Wilhelminapark, Tilburg' (https://www.monumentaltrees.com/nl/nld/noordbrabant/tilburg/2357_wilhelminapark/41192/); the page itself could not be fetched directly (monumentaltrees.com 403s automated fetches, per data/fetch-blocklist.json), so treat only the page's existence/title as corroboration of species+location, not any measurement reported about it

trees.name: The Twin Planes of the Stadhuis
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from the register's 1860-1870 planting band, matching an independent 2018 estimate of about 170 years old

location.address: Stadhuisplein 128, behind the Paleis-Raadhuis (the oldest wing of Tilburg's town hall)

trees.story:
In 2018 a growth-site study commissioned by the municipality reached a conclusion about one of these two plane trees: it could not be sustainably preserved through the rebuilding of Tilburg's town hall. It was one of some forty trees on the site marked to come down, and the objection that followed was loud and public. The work ran until February 2021.

Two months after it finished, a dated account from the Stadhuisplein described what was standing there: two plane trees, both dating from around 1850, both still on the municipality's monumental tree list, at the old palace-town hall.

So the best evidence is that the tree service's own worry did not come true and the pair came through the building work. What we cannot do is prove it for today. Nothing we found from 2022 onward counts the trees at this spot, so if you walk past and there is one where this page says two, tell us and the entry gets corrected.

The national register treats the pair as one entry, two trees at a single point, which is also how they read on the ground: two trunks, one place to stand, behind the oldest wing of the Stadhuis. It dates the planting to between 1860 and 1870. The 2018 study called them about 170 years old. The 2021 account put them at around 1850. Three estimates agreeing to within about twenty years, and not one of them made by anybody who was there.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by there being two of them, a matched pair of planes with the flaking, patchwork bark of the species. They stand on the Stadhuisplein at the Paleis-Raadhuis, the oldest wing of Tilburg's town hall.

http://vogelsenzo.blogspot.com/2021/04/plataan.html (dated April 2021, after the Stadhuis/Stadskantoor renovation finished in February 2021; independently describes two common plane trees, circa 1850, standing in front of the old palace-town hall, both on the municipality's monumental tree list)
